[38;5;246m[48;5;237m❯ [38;5;231mWrite a 600 word essay about terminal multiplexers. Use no tools.[39m

[38;5;231m[49m⏺[39m Terminal multiplexers solve a problem that most developers face every day: a single terminal window is not enough to hold all the work happening at once. A typical session might include a development server, a test
  watcher, a database shell, a log tail, and an editor, all of which need to stay open and visible. Before multiplexers, the usual answer was to open a dozen terminal windows or tabs, each one a separate process that
  vanished the moment the window closed. Terminal multiplexers offer a different model, one in which the workspace lives on a server-side process and the terminal is merely a window onto it.

  The two most widely used multiplexers are tmux and GNU Screen. Screen arrived first, in the late 1980s, and it established the core idea: a long-running process that owns pseudo-terminals and can be detached from one
  terminal and reattached to another. tmux, written in the 2000s as a more modern alternative, kept that model but improved on its design. It offers a cleaner command language, a configuration system built around a
  single file, splits and windows that can be arranged freely, and a scripting interface that makes it practical to build repeatable layouts. Both tools share the same essential trick: the shell processes keep running
  whether or not anyone is watching them.

  The practical value of this design is easiest to see when a connection drops. Anyone who has run a long compilation or a data migration over SSH knows the frustration of a dropped network link killing the job midway.
  With a multiplexer, the job runs inside a session on the remote machine. If the connection fails, the session continues. The user reconnects, attaches to the existing session, and resumes exactly where they left off,
